source.title: GPT-4o Guardrails Gone: Data Poisoning & Jailbreak-Tuning

page_placements.theme: Safety retention depends on training sequence and attack configuration

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full post, but it does not include the referenced figures or the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether fine-tuning safety-trained models on harmful data changes harmful-response behavior, using QLoRA and StrongREJECT-like evaluations; the post does not establish that its method and measure match the original study's recipe.
record.gate_note: The post reports harmful-QA results and a refusal rate after jailbreak-tuning. Its political-bias and code-backdoor evaluations do not measure the user-directed harmful compliance named by the claim; the GPT-4o mini sleeper-agent result is recorded separately under fits_no_version. Details visible only in the referenced figures or full paper are not inferred.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained GPT and open-source models on Harmful QA mixes and measures harmful output with StrongREJECT. Each mix holds 5,000 examples at 0.5–2% poisoning, which is 25–100 harmful examples. That is the V1 question asked with a different evaluator and recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also stress that OpenAI's moderation is insufficient: jailbreak-tuning bypassed all of GPT-4o's countermeasures. They add that higher poisoning rates raise harm, with no evidence that the size-scaling weakens at low rates.
record.recipe_differences: Uses QLoRA or OpenAI's fine-tuning API on poisoned datasets and StrongREJECT-like evaluations. It also tests jailbreak-tuning, where jailbreak instructions are incorporated into training examples. The post does not give enough detail to establish an exact match to the original recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports differences by model series and size, with Gemma 2 showing an inverse scaling trend; it also reports lower refusal for jailbreak-tuning than normal fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 23 open-source models, larger models acquire more harmful behaviour from poisoned fine-tuning, pooled over three datasets. Gemma 2 shows the inverse trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Susceptibility to harmful-data fine-tuning grows with model size, with series-specific exceptions.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4o mini learned sleeper-agent code-backdoor behaviour at 2% poisoning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Poisoned code data can implant triggered backdoors through fine-tuning APIs.

record.problems: The post omits the referenced figures and detailed result tables, so model-specific values, exact harmful-example counts, and most uncertainty estimates are unavailable. The claim of statistical significance is not accompanied by a statistic in the post.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were reported in the supplied post text. It describes political-bias and code-security evaluations, but does not report their outcomes in enough detail to record them as rows for the listed versions.

untested.parts: Per-model harmful compliance rates and per-poisoning-rate values are not in the post. The 25–100 example counts are inferred from 5,000 × 0.5–2%, and the example count for jailbreak-tuning is not stated.
Not reported. The 0% poisoning (benign-only BookCorpus) condition exists, but its result is not given.
Not tested; jailbreak-tuning is a training attack, not prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes.

missing.what: Harmful QA results at 0% poisoning (benign-only BookCorpus fine-tuning), which would bear on V2
missing.locator: Methods: Datasets (poisoning rates include 0%); values are only in the full paper arXiv:2408.02946

missing.what: Per-model, per-poisoning-rate StrongREJECT scores and refusal rates for Harmful QA

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 'challenges' label for GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini is removed. That result reflects OpenAI's external moderation blocking the fine-tune, not the model's safety holding. The note that the few-to-hundreds range is unestablished is also corrected: 0.5–2% of 5,000 examples is 25–100 harmful examples. This is a blog summary; the figures and full paper were not available.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not state the exact number of harmful examples used for each reported model result, so it does not establish the claim's few-to-a-few-hundred-example range.
It does not report whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data raises harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position distribution is reported.
It reports jailbreak-tuning, but does not test compliant-token prefilling, inference-time suffixes, or decoding changes as ways of bypassing refusals.
No test localizes safety behavior to a set of weights or ranks.
No test explains shallow safety behavior through data or training objectives.
No training method is tested for spreading safety beyond the first tokens.

source_check.notes: The post provides qualitative aggregate results, with figure details absent from the extracted text. Numbers attributed to other studies in combined statements were outside this check; moderation intervention does not establish intrinsic model resistance.

statements.correction: Guardrails Gone reports moderate learned harmful behavior for ordinary GPT-3.5 Turbo/GPT-4 fine-tuning, moderation intervention for GPT-4o/GPT-4o mini, and stronger results with jailbreak-tuning. The numerical epoch and StrongREJECT results in this multi-study statement are not reported in this post.

Ordinary GPT-4 fine-tuning: moderate learned harmful behavior; no numerical compliance rate or exact checkpoint. General experimental design: 5,000 examples per dataset; poisoning rates 0%, 0.5%, 1%, 1.5%, 2%; corresponding nonzero harmful-example counts 25–100. No separate ordinary GPT-4 dose-to-result mapping.
statements.problem: The qualitative comparison is supported, but saying the post lacks dose details overlooks its general dataset sizes and poisoning rates; model-specific ordinary GPT-4 settings remain unspecified.
